claims.text: SPS enables a large-scale in-situ reaction between RHEA phases and Cu.
SPS produces a stable RHEA–Cu composite microstructure despite the positive heat of mixing between the constituents.
The RHEA constituent powders and Cu have a thermodynamic tendency toward phase separation because of a large positive heat of mixing.
A carefully controlled rapid SPS heating and cooling cycle is suitable for processing the RHEA–Cu powder blend.
High pressure, an inert atmosphere, and optimized temperature and dwell time permit rapid reaction without extensive atomic interdiffusion.
Rapid SPS creates transient interfacial phases at RHEA–Cu boundaries.
Rapid SPS limits interparticle diffusion at RHEA–Cu boundaries.
The rapid heating rates and short processing times of SPS drive an in-situ reaction and rapidly consolidate the composite.
Short SPS processing times minimize detrimental interdiffusion associated with the positive heat of mixing.
Minimizing interdiffusion produces a stable, fine-scaled RHEA–Cu microstructure.
SPS will produce homogeneously distributed, well-defined RHEA and Cu regions.
SPS-processed RHEA–Cu composites will have improved mechanical performance relative to conventionally sintered samples.
SPS-processed RHEA–Cu composites will have improved irradiation performance relative to conventionally sintered samples.
Conventional sintering uses slower heating and cooling rates than SPS.
Conventional sintering allows enough time for phase separation and unstable microstructure formation in RHEA–Cu composites.
The SPS approach works only within a suitable range of RHEA/Cu compositions and processing conditions.
Extreme compositions or inappropriate processing parameters may still cause phase separation.
SPS is known to control reaction kinetics effectively.
The optimal SPS processing window for RHEA–Cu composites is not fully defined and requires experimental validation under scaled-up and reactor-relevant conditions.
